name: Nanofat / autologous fat grafting
lead: Fat transfer, also called fat grafting or lipofilling, moves a person's own fat, usually harvested by liposuction, to another area to restore volume or smooth irregularities. In the face it is used to refill hollow areas such as the lower eyelid and perioral region, and it is also used for the breasts, buttocks, hands and scars.[1] Nanofat is a variant in which fat is mechanically emulsified and filtered into a thin liquid that can be injected through very fine needles. Surgeons use it for skin quality, fine wrinkles, discolouration and scars rather than for volume.[2][3]

The technique was described in 2013 by the Belgian plastic surgeon Patrick Tonnard and colleagues in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.[2][15] Its proposed mechanism is that the emulsified fat contains no intact fat cells but retains stromal vascular fraction cells, including adipose-derived stem cells, which are thought to support tissue repair.[2][4] Published clinical work consists mostly of case series and small comparative studies, and a 2024 systematic review of twelve studies described most as low level of evidence while reporting improved scars and skin quality and no severe complications.[5]

People discussing facial aesthetics encounter nanofat as one of several options for under-eye hollows, scars and skin texture, alongside fillers, platelet-rich plasma and lasers. Fat transfer is also one of the procedures that some forum members list among the surgeries in an overall facial plan.[6][7]

paras: Fat grafting has three stages: harvesting, processing and reinjection. It can be done under local or general anaesthesia, and the donor fat typically comes from areas where liposuction is practical. Wikipedia lists the advantages cited for autologous fat as biocompatibility and ready availability, and notes that the fat should not be manipulated too much and should be reinjected quickly to improve survival.[1]

In facial surgery, fat transfer restores volume lost with age. It is used in the periorbital area and around the mouth, and micro fat transplantation is used in rhinoplasty to correct a low nasal dorsum. In scars from injury, burns or acne, fat grafting is reported to soften and thicken the skin.[1] Variants named in the literature include macrofat, microfat, nanofat and stromal vascular fraction gel, which differ in particle size and processing.[4][5]

In the original 2013 description, fat harvested by liposuction is processed into microfat and then passed back and forth between syringes through a narrow connector and filtered, producing a liquid that can be injected with needles up to 27 gauge. Because it is so fluid, it can be placed superficially in the skin, for example along fine lines, in scars and in the dark lower eyelid, which thicker fat grafts do not reach well.[2][15]

The authors compared standard lipoaspirate, microfat and nanofat in the laboratory. The nanofat contained no viable fat cells but still had many adipose-derived stem cells, which proliferated and differentiated in culture similarly to those in the other samples.[2] In the 67 patients in the clinical part of the report, skin quality improved at six months with no infections, fat cysts or granulomas reported.[2]

A 2016 study of mechanical shear on the stromal vascular fraction examined which progenitor cell populations survive emulsification, and a 2019 review used the term micro-fragmented fat for nanofat alongside stromal vascular fraction, adipose-derived stem cells and extracellular vesicles as adipose-derived products used in dermatology and aesthetic rejuvenation.[4][14]

sections.h: Patrick Tonnard and the origin of the technique
paras: Patrick Tonnard is a plastic surgeon in Ghent, Belgium. He graduated from Ghent University in 1987, has been a consultant at AZ Sint-Lucas Hospital since 1994, and with Alexis Verpaele developed the MACS-lift, a short-scar facelift published in 2002. He completed a PhD on fat grafting for facial rejuvenation at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel in 2015.[15]

His team's 2013 nanofat report was followed by the 2017 book Centrofacial Rejuvenation, which covers nanofat grafting and, according to Belgian broadcaster VRT NWS as cited by Wikipedia, received a British Medical Association Medical Book Award in 2018, and by Regenerative Facial Surgery in 2022.[15] The 2013 paper has been cited several hundred times, and later groups have developed modified versions of the process.[2][16]

The original 2013 report described nanofat grafting in 67 cases for superficial problems and presented preliminary cell-content findings, with improved skin quality at six months.[2] A 2018 Aesthetic Surgery Journal analysis of 52 patients treated between November 2013 and April 2016 covered scars (40 of the treated defects), wrinkles and discolouration and reported marked improvement of scar quality and high patient satisfaction.[3]

A 2017 comparative study tested three modified nanofat procedures, supercharged, evo and centrifuged, against the classic method on scars; the supercharged version produced the best clinical outcomes and the highest stromal vascular fraction yield, and the authors concluded that cell yield correlated with outcome.[16] A 2018 case series of 20 patients with 25 atrophic facial scars combined condensed nanofat with fat grafts; patient-rated and observer-rated scar scores both fell significantly, and sebaceous and sweat glands were seen on histology after surgery.[17]

Other published work covers unfiltered nanofat for post-burn facial scars and facial rejuvenation with nanofat grafts.[18][19] A 2022 randomised, single-blinded split-face trial in seven patients with acne scars compared nanofat alone with nanofat plus stromal vascular fraction; both sides improved, and the authors reported larger dermal thickness gains on the combined side at one month.[20]

A 2024 systematic review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery included twelve studies. Six studies with 253 patients reported improved scar characteristics, four reported skin rejuvenation effects such as reduced wrinkles and pigmentation changes, histology showed increases in skin thickness, collagen and elastic fibres, and the authors noted no severe complications. They also noted that no meta-analysis was possible because of clinical heterogeneity and that studies generally had a low level of evidence.[5]

Registered trials include post-burn facial scars (48 participants), atrophic scars (20), nanofat injection versus nanofat with microneedling in scars (30), infraorbital rejuvenation compared with platelet-poor plasma gel (60), and nanofat for androgenetic alopecia (10) and female pattern hair loss (40).[8][9][10][11][12][13] Controlled effect sizes for most appearance uses have not been reported.

Under-eye area: nanofat has been studied for dark circles and fine lines of the lower eyelid, and a registered trial compares it with platelet-poor plasma gel for tear-trough rejuvenation.[2][11] Scars: acne, burn and traumatic scars are the best-represented indication in the literature.[3][5][16][17][18] Skin quality: reviews describe improved texture, pigmentation and fine wrinkles after nanofat.[5][14] Hair: small registered trials have tested nanofat for hair loss.[12][13]
A 2024 systematic review also lists experimental studies, not yet clinical evidence, on fat graft survival, diabetic wound healing and hair growth.[5]

For fat grafting generally, Wikipedia lists swelling, bruising, hematoma, donor-site pain or altered sensation, hypertrophic scarring, infection, contour irregularities, injury from cannulas and fat necrosis; it says up to 50 percent of transferred fat may be reabsorbed in breast augmentation.[1] The 2013 nanofat report and the 2024 systematic review reported no severe complications in the studies they covered, which were small.[2][5]
The procedure also involves a liposuction donor site and anaesthesia.[1]

On looksmax.org, threads compare fat transfer with fillers for the tear trough and nasolabial folds, ask why fat transfer around the eyes is discussed so rarely, and ask about topical products marketed as lipofilling agents, which are a different category from surgical fat grafting.[6][7][21] Posters describing multi-surgery plans, such as combined jaw surgery, rhinoplasty, hair transplant and fat transfer, treat fat transfer as one item among several facial procedures.[22]
Nanofat itself is discussed far less than filler or fat transfer, and most reader-facing information comes from clinic websites and surgeon publications rather than community guides.

timeline.event: Patrick Tonnard graduates in medicine at Ghent University.[15]
Tonnard and Verpaele publish the MACS-lift facelift.[15]
Nanofat grafting described in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, with 67 clinical cases and laboratory comparison to microfat.[2]
Tonnard completes a PhD on fat grafting for facial rejuvenation.[15]
A comparison of modified nanofat procedures on scars links stromal vascular fraction yield to clinical outcome; Centrofacial Rejuvenation published.[15][16]
An Aesthetic Surgery Journal analysis of 52 patients and a JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery series on atrophic scars are published.[3][17]
Review of adipose-derived therapies in dermatology and aesthetic rejuvenation published; unfiltered nanofat for post-burn facial scars reported.[14][18]
Randomised split-face trial of stromal vascular fraction added to nanofat in acne scars published.[20]
Systematic review of twelve nanofat studies published in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery; new scar trials registered.[5][9][10]

lore.intro: Fat transfer and lipofilling come up on looksmax.org as alternatives or complements to fillers for hollows under the eyes and around the nose and mouth.[6][7][21]

claims.claim: Fat transfer gives a more natural, longer-lasting fill than filler
claims.believers: Forum posters compare fat transfer with fillers for facial hollows and ask why the option is discussed less often.[7][21]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes autologous fat as biocompatible and widely available, and notes that part of transferred fat may be reabsorbed, with figures up to 50 percent cited for breast augmentation.[1]

claims.claim: Nanofat improves scars and skin texture
claims.believers: Clinics and surgeons using nanofat report softer scars and improved skin quality; the original authors reported improvement at six months.[2][3]
claims.experts: A 2024 systematic review reported improved scars and skin quality in small studies of low level of evidence, with no severe complications.[5]

claims.believers: The proposed mechanism is that stromal vascular fraction and adipose-derived stem cells in the emulsion support repair.[2][4]
claims.experts: A 2017 study found that stromal vascular fraction yield correlated with scar outcomes, and a 2022 split-face trial of seven patients found added stromal vascular fraction increased dermal thickness at one month; reviewers note the evidence base is small.[16][20]

claims.claim: Nanofat can treat under-eye dark circles
claims.believers: The original report included the dark lower eyelid among treated areas.[2]
claims.experts: A trial of nanofat versus platelet-poor plasma gel for infraorbital rejuvenation is registered; published controlled results have not been reported.[11]

claims.believers: Small registered trials have tested nanofat for androgenetic alopecia and female pattern hair loss.[12][13]
claims.experts: The 2024 systematic review lists hair growth among experimental findings and calls for clinical studies.[5]

claims.claim: Topical 'lipofilling agents' reproduce the effect of fat transfer
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread discusses a topical product marketed to increase fat in hollow areas under the eye and around the nasolabial folds.[21]
claims.experts: No clinical studies of topical lipofilling agents were found in the literature reviewed here; surgical fat grafting is a distinct procedure.[1]

card.summary: Emulsified own-fat injections for scars and skin quality; published work is mostly small clinical series.
card.note: Surgical procedure; fat reabsorption and necrosis are reported.

quick.overview:
Fat transfer moves a person's own fat to another area. Nanofat is an emulsified, filtered form used for scars and skin texture.

Published studies are mostly small series and uncontrolled reports.
quick.mechanism: Liposuctioned fat is processed and reinjected; for nanofat, the liquid contains stromal vascular cells proposed to aid tissue repair.
quick.risks: Reported effects include swelling, bruising, donor-site pain, infection, contour irregularities and fat necrosis.
